description: Equipo orientado a la salud astronauta
summary:
We developed VITALIS, a software prototype for monitoring astronaut health during long-duration missions. It integrates physiological indicators, sleep and emotional well-being records, and environmental variables such as temperature, pressure, and radiation.
To address the challenge, VITALIS compares indicators against a personal baseline, accounts for physical activity, and combines alert rules with artificial intelligence models to identify deviations and forecast trends. Results are presented through a dashboard featuring a 3D body visualization, individual health history, and an assistant that explains alerts and suggests follow-up actions. The prototype uses synthetic data generated by simulators, including ASTROSIM on an ESP32, and supports the integration of selected physical sensor measurements. Its models and thresholds require clinical validation.
Its importance lies in helping astronauts understand their condition, recognize changes requiring attention, and make informed decisions. Through local processing, VITALIS aims to strengthen crew autonomy and support health management in isolated and demanding environments.
details:
We developed VITALIS, a software prototype that brings together information about an astronaut’s health and presents it in an easy-to-understand way. Its purpose is to help astronauts recognize changes in their body, sleep, and emotional well-being, alongside environmental conditions that could affect their health during a space mission.

How does it work?

VITALIS receives data such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, temperature, and movement. It also incorporates sleep, mood, and fatigue records, along with environmental variables such as oxygen levels, pressure, and radiation.

The information can come from sensors connected to an ESP32 or from simulators. To test the project, we use ASTROSIM, a program that lets us adjust values and recreate different situations. For example, we can simulate rising temperature or decreasing oxygen levels and observe how VITALIS responds.

The system first checks whether the readings have sufficient quality. It then identifies each astronaut’s usual values and uses them as a personal baseline to detect changes. It also considers physical activity, because an increased heart rate during exercise requires a different interpretation from the same increase at rest.

To analyze the data, VITALIS combines programmed rules with artificial intelligence models. These help identify unusual patterns and estimate how certain variables might change over the next few seconds.

Results appear on a dashboard with graphs, individual history, and a 3D body visualization. When an alert occurs, the system identifies what changed, and an assistant explains the notification in plain language.

What benefits does it offer, and what impact do we expect?

VITALIS brings different indicators together in one tool and allows users to track changes over time. This helps astronauts better understand their condition and identify situations that require further attention.

The intended impact is to strengthen crew autonomy during long-duration missions, especially when communication with Earth is difficult. Data processing and storage take place locally. To make the entire interface work without internet access, we still need to include some externally loaded visual resources within the project.

What tools did we use?

  • Python, FastAPI, NumPy, and scikit-learn: to receive and analyze data and run artificial intelligence models.
  • SQLite: to store readings and each astronaut’s history.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: to build the web interface.
  • Three.js and Chart.js: to display the 3D body and graphs.
  • ESP32 and C++ programming with Arduino: to connect sensors and transmit information over Wi-Fi.
  • MAX30102, TMP117, and MPU6050 sensors: to obtain heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, contact temperature, and movement measurements.
  • ASTROSIM and an internal simulator: to test scenarios without depending on a complete set of physical sensors.
  • Ollama, optionally: to help the assistant phrase explanations more naturally.

What makes the project creative?

VITALIS connects information about the body, personal well-being, and the environment to provide a combined view of an astronaut’s condition. Beyond displaying numbers, it explains changes and compares them with what is usual for that individual.

Integration with ASTROSIM allows us to adjust test conditions and demonstrate how a reading becomes an understandable alert. This helps us evaluate and improve the prototype.

What factors did we consider?

We considered differences between individuals, changes caused by exercise, measurement errors, movement, and missing data. For this reason, the system checks signal quality before interpreting readings.

We also prioritized clear presentation and local operation. Currently, the models are trained on synthetic data, and the alert thresholds are provisional. The prototype demonstrates how the proposed approach works; using it as a medical tool will require validation with real data and qualified specialists.
